claims.value: Bodart gives side B (Prussian) as the garrison of 2,400 men with 92 guns under Colonel v. Ingersleben, and side A (French) as 1,500 French under Brigadier General Gauthier, to whom the garrison surrendered without striking a blow. claims.value: Side B (Prussian) in Höpfner: by 30 October 80 guns stood on the walls, supplied with 200 rounds, and 12 more in reserve. Besides a sufficient number of artillerymen the garrison was the 3rd musketeer battalions of the regiments Oranien, Zenge and Prinz Heinrich and 75 hussars of the regiment Usedom under Rittmeister Kalbow, who had come from Merseburg and stayed at Küstrin by the King's order: in all about 2400 men, of whom 1600 were fully fit for service. At the commandant's council Colonel Weyherr said that his battalion had very many untrained men, and the engineer lieutenant Thynkel that the fortress could defend itself with 1600 men and sufficient guns.

claims.value: Höpfner: Davout detached Gudin's division against Küstrin to seize its bridgehead if possible. After the fight at the bridgehead Gudin summoned the fortress and let the commandant know that he would bombard the town if surrender were refused; recalled that night, he left only the 85th regiment under General Gauthier. When the commandant's envoy, Lieutenant Thynkel, came to negotiate an armistice, General Petit seemed willing to negotiate, but Colonel Düplin of the 85th declared that unless the town were surrendered within 2 hours the bombardment would begin. Gauthier and Düplin received the commandant and told him that Stettin had fallen, Hohenlohe's corps was captured and Küstrin badly garrisoned, and that the bombardment would begin at once and not stop until the town was in ashes; the French general dictated the terms, and grenadiers crossing the Oder soon occupied the fortress. Davout then went to Küstrin in person (OCR passage). The 25th Bulletin: Davout had Küstrin invested and summoned.
claims.rationale: Höpfner from the page images of pp. 324-328, with his sentence on Davout from the OCR; the Bulletin from the page image of p. 648. By Höpfner's account the summons, the threats and the dictated terms were the French commanders' own steps at Küstrin; the move on Küstrin was Davout's order (claim posture). Höpfner does not say which general dictated the terms. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'with the main body of the corps Marshal Davout set out on the 28th from the area in front of Berlin, and on the 29th detached from Müncheberg the division Güdin with 12 guns on Küstrin, to seize the bridgehead there if possible'; 'General Güdin summoned the fortress and let the commandant know that he would bombard the town if the surrender were refused'; 'in the night before 1 November General Güdin received the order to set out at once for the main body of the 3rd corps at Frankfurt, as Napoleon would set part of Marshal Augereau's troops marching to Küstrin and assign them to invest the fortress'; 'General Güdin had to comply with the order, set out at daybreak on 1 November, and left behind only the 85th infantry regiment under General Gauthier'; 'Lieutenant Thynkel believed he had to obey, met the first French post at the far end of the suburb, and was taken to General Petit, who was about to have the posts relieved'; 'the general seemed willing to enter into negotiations, but was prevented from it by Colonel Düplin of the 85th regiment, who was present and declared: if the town were not surrendered within 2 hours, the bombardment would begin'; 'the commandant was received on the other side by General Gauthier and Colonel Düplin; it was put to him that Stettin had fallen, the Hohenlohe corps was captured, Küstrin badly garrisoned, the bombardment would begin at once and not stop until the town had been reduced to ashes. The commandant'; 'the French general dictated the points of capitulation, by which at noon on 1 November the gates were to be occupied by 3 companies of French grenadiers, the garrison was to lay down its arms, safeguards were to be granted to the members of the Chamber and the property of the inhabitants protected. Lieutenant Thynkel refused his signature'; 'immediately after the signing the commandant crossed back over the Oder accompanied by Colonel Düplin and two soldiers, and in a short time the fortress was occupied by grenadiers crossing over'; 'Marshal Davout went at once in person to Küstrin, had the bridges restored and made all arrangements so that the following corps should profit from the unexpected conquest of a fortified place on the Oder, which together with Stettin offered an excellent base for the further operations against the Vistula' (OCR); the Bulletin, as in claim side-b-strength-french.

claims.value: Höpfner: Colonel Ingersleben, the commandant, had been ordered on 17 October to make all defensive arrangements to secure the fortress against a forcible attack. In the fight at the bridgehead the Prussians escaped over the bridge he had already set on fire. That evening, when bugles sounded at the end of the Oder bridge, he told the engineer of the place, Lieutenant Thynkel, to go over and ask what the alarm meant and to threaten to burn the suburbs; when Thynkel objected to threatening or negotiating with the enemy, he sent the artillery lieutenant Wille to agree that if the enemy kept quiet he would not fire on the bridgehead. On the morning of 1 November he told his staff officers that he had sure news of a corps of 100,000 men approaching on the right bank, that no relief was to be expected and that the state of the garrison was known to all. Colonel Weyherr advised surrender rather than see the suburbs burned, Colonel Manteuffel agreed, trusting the commandant to act on his instructions, Colonel Boumann of the artillery said the commandant could do as he pleased, and Thynkel held that the fortress must and could defend itself, the main wall holding even without the outworks, and that a bombardment would not take it, the garrison having casemates. The commandant declared that he would not have the town burned and sent Thynkel to negotiate an armistice of 8 to 14 days; on Thynkel's report he said there was no time to lose and went himself, his wife's pleas being set aside by the Küstrin Kammerpräsident, who had gained great influence over him. Received by Gauthier and Düplin, he let himself be moved to capitulate, answering Thynkel's objections that he knew the Grand Duke of Berg was approaching with 100,000 men, after which no capitulation would be possible, and that he must not let the town be burned or its citizens made unhappy. Thynkel refused to sign. A court martial sentenced Ingersleben to be shot for proven cowardice; the King pardoned him to fortress imprisonment for life.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 325-328. Höpfner does not name his sources for this passage. A Kammerpräsident was the president of a provincial chamber (Kammer). English renderings (ours): 'the commandant of Küstrin, Colonel Ingersleben, received on 17 October the order to make all defensive arrangements to secure the fortress against a forcible attack'; as in claim side-b-losses for the fight at the bridgehead; 'still in the evening at 6 o'clock bugles were heard repeatedly in the fortress at the'; 'end of the Oder bridge'; 'the commandant charged the engineer of the place, Lieutenant Thynkel, to go across and ask what the alarm meant; he would, if the enemy did not keep quiet, have the suburbs set on fire'; 'Lieutenant Thynkel represented to him how unfitting it was to threaten the enemy, and to negotiate with him at all'; 'instead of him the commandant now sent the artillery lieutenant Wille across to come to an understanding with the enemy that if they kept quiet, he, the commandant, would not have the bridgehead fired on'; 'Colonel Ingersleben assembled the staff officers of the garrison on the morning of 1 November and put it to them that the enemy was before the gates of the fortress, and that he had received sure news that a corps of 100,000 men was also on the march on the right bank of the Oder; relief was not to be expected; the state of the garrison was known to all'; as in claim side-b-strength for Colonel Weyherr; 'Colonel Manteuffel of the regiment Zenge likewise voted for the surrender, relying on the honesty of the commandant to act according to the instruction given him'; 'Colonel Boumann of the'; 'artillery, who was present, answered: the commandant could do and leave undone what he would'; as in claim side-b-strength for Lieutenant Thynkel; 'the commandant objected that the garrison was not enough to man the outworks, to which Lieutenant Thynkel replied that even after abandoning the outworks the main wall could hold sufficiently'; claims.value: Bodart records the capitulation of Küstrin on 1 November: the Prussian garrison surrendered without striking a blow to the French under Gauthier and was led away as prisoners of war, the officers being released on parole. Höpfner dates it 1 November: by the terms the French general dictated, the gates were to be occupied at noon by 3 companies of French grenadiers, the garrison was to lay down its arms, the members of the Chamber were to be granted safeguards and the inhabitants' property protected; grenadiers crossing the Oder soon occupied the fortress, and the garrison, assembled in the market square, threw down its arms. The Emperor wrote on 2 November that Küstrin had surrendered the day before; the 25th Bulletin, that Davout had it invested and summoned and it surrendered, the officers returning home on parole and the soldiers being taken to France.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome with Höpfner's account and the French documents, read from the page images; no source read gives a different result. Bodart's 'without striking a blow' describes the capitulation; he does not mention the fight at the bridgehead the day before (claim side-b-losses). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength, and 'the garrison was led away as prisoners of war, officers released on their word of honour'; Höpfner, 'capitulation of Küstrin on 1 November'; as in claim side-a-command for the terms and the occupation; 'the garrison, assembled on the market square, threw their muskets, pouches and sabres on the ground, partly in indignation, partly with cheering and shouting, and Colonel Ingersleben, heaped with the reproaches of the subaltern officers, had to escape from the market square'; the Emperor and the Bulletin, as in claim side-b-strength-french.

claims.value: Bodart places Küstrin, a town in Brandenburg, at the confluence of the Warthe and the Oder, 25 km north-east of Frankfurt an der Oder. Höpfner: the fortress had a main wall, palisaded outworks and casemates, and a bridgehead covered by abatis and wolf pits; Gudin's advance guard met the Prussian hussars at Manschenow on the left bank of the Oder and drove them into the bridgehead, from which the Prussians escaped over a bridge the commandant had already set on fire; the first French post stood at the far end of the suburb, and the commandant, about to have himself ferried over the Oder, was received on the other side by General Gauthier and Colonel Düplin. The 25th Bulletin calls the place in very good condition and situated in the middle of the marshes.
claims.rationale: Location and works as described, read from the page images; no plan of Küstrin was inspected, and where each work stood is taken only from the narrative. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(town in Prussia, Brandenburg, at the confluence of the Warthe with the Oder, 25 km north-east of Frankfurt an der Oder)'; Höpfner, as in claims side-b-strength for the walls, outworks and bridgehead, side-b-losses for Manschenow and the bridge, side-b-command for the main wall, the casemates and the commandant's crossing, and side-a-command for the first French post and the commandant's reception; the Bulletin, 'the place, in very good condition, is situated in the middle of the marshes; it holds considerable magazines. It is one of the most important conquests of the army; it has completed making us masters of all the places on the Oder'.

open_questions: Deferred: a French report of the capitulation (a search of the Foucart t. II OCR for Küstrin, Gauthier, Ingersleben and Duplin found none besides the Emperor's letter and the 25th Bulletin; Davout's own correspondence, a further family, was not read); a return of Gudin's division and of the 85th regiment; the capitulation's text; the record of the court martial, which Höpfner does not cite; the rest of the Emperor's letter (Foucart t. II, p. 617). Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated: the date of Napoleon's order sending the Baden contingent to occupy the fortress (Höpfner, p. 328) and a later Bulletin's figure for the magazines found at Küstrin (Foucart t. II, p. 667), seen in the search.

Most consequential gap: side A's strength at the capitulation. Bodart gives 1,500 French under Gauthier; Höpfner names only the 85th regiment, left under Gauthier when Gudin's division and its 12 guns were recalled, and gives no strength; the Bulletin credits Davout with investing the place. A return of the 85th for 1 November could settle it, and with it whether a garrison of about 2400 (Höpfner) surrendered to a single regiment.

Disputes kept as separate claims: the garrison (about 2400 with 1600 fit, Höpfner; 2,400, Bodart; 4,000 prisoners, the Emperor and the Bulletin); the guns (80 on the walls and 12 in reserve, Höpfner, 92 by our arithmetic; 92, Bodart; 80, the Emperor; 90, the Bulletin); side A (1,500 under Gauthier, Bodart; the 85th regiment under Gauthier after Gudin's division left, Höpfner); who summoned the place (Gudin, Höpfner; Davout, the Bulletin); and Bodart's 'without striking a blow' against Höpfner's fight at the bridgehead on 31 October, in which Lieutenant Falkenhayn was shot dead.

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked, though his 2,400 men and 92 guns are Höpfner's about 2400 and his 80 and 12 guns, by our arithmetic); Foucart, t. II (the French side's documents: the Emperor's letter to the Grand Duke of Berg and the 25th Bulletin, both of 2 November, from the page images; the Bulletin repeats the Emperor's 4,000 prisoners but gives 90 guns to his 80); Höpfner, Bd. 2, 2nd edition (the Prussian side's history; by the preface of his first volume the work rests chiefly on the records of the judicial inquiries held after the war, but the Küstrin passage names no source).
